The cane toad (Rhinella marina) exhibits a remarkable life history that begins with an extraordinarily small neonate. Newly hatched individuals emerge from the jelly-coated egg at a wet weight of only 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a figure derived from the egg diameter of approximately two millimeters, with the chorion rupture occurring after a relatively brief developmental period. When maintained at a constant temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the embryonated eggs hatch after about 11 days [ab = about 11 days], reflecting the rapid embryonic development typical of this invasive bufonid. The tiny tadpoles that emerge are initially lecithotrophic, relying on residual yolk stores before transitioning to active filter feeding. This modest birth mass stands in stark contrast to the enormous size females can ultimately achieve, as fully grown, reproductively active adult females can reach an ultimate wet weight of 1500 grams [Wwi = 1500 grams], representing one of the largest body sizes recorded among anurans. The extraordinary disparity between hatching mass and adult mass underscores the prodigious growth trajectory this species undertakes during its aquatic larval phase and subsequent terrestrial juvenile stage.

The gelatinous egg masses are typically deposited in shallow, ephemeral water bodies where the melanised eggs benefit from some thermal buffering. This massive reproductive investment is energetically demanding and likely contributes to the relatively short lifespan observed in wild populations, as females channel substantial resources into gamete production rather than somatic maintenance. The strategy of producing vast numbers of small offspring, each starting at a minimal birth mass, is a classic r-selected life history tactic that facilitates rapid population expansion.

From a comparative physiological perspective, the life history parameters of Rhinella marina reveal several adaptations that facilitate its invasion success across diverse habitats. The combination of a minute hatchling mass of just 4.2 milligrams [Wwb = 4.2 milligrams] with an adult female mass approaching 1.5 kilograms [Wwi = 1.5 kilograms] represents a weight gain of over 350,000-fold, one of the most extreme ontogenetic size increases documented among terrestrial vertebrates.
